1170.title: The dark age is a knife
1170.word: The dark age is a knife
1170.hook: this age is a knife, kings are butchers, and righteousness has flown (Majh ki Var, ang 145)
1170.tomorrow: Hard to be called a Muslim
1170.howItsDone: This salok is sung and read as part of Majh ki Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in katha it is explained as Guru Nanak's plain speech about rulers and the darkness of falsehood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the majh ballad: Guru Nanak's var in steps, sung to an old tune, opening with the Guru as giver, ice and lamp. Today it reaches one of its hardest lines.

The age is a knife. The kings are butchers. Righteousness has grown wings and flown away. That's one salok in Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, in plain English, not word for word. It doesn't sound like a hymn. It sounds like a headline: no soft opening, just three blunt pictures, one after another. And then, in the next breath, the lights go out.
screen: `THE AGE IS A KNIFE.` → `THE KINGS ARE BUTCHERS.` → `RIGHTEOUSNESS HAS FLOWN.`

segments.voice: The age is Kal, the Kali Yuga, the dark age in the old Indian reckoning of time, and Guru Nanak makes it a blade. The salok goes on, again in plain English: falsehood is the night of the new moon, and the moon of truth can't be seen rising anywhere. I've searched and searched, and I'm bewildered. In the darkness there's no path to be seen. People cry out in pain, caught in their own ego. Says Nanak, how will anyone be saved? Three things to notice. First, he names who holds the knife. Not demons, not fate: kings, the people trusted with power. The Babarvani hymns, a few days back, said something like it about an invasion; here it widens into a picture of an age. Second, righteousness isn't killed. It flies. It grows wings and leaves, which means it was able to go, and might be able to return. Third, Nanak puts himself in the dark too. He doesn't stand above the age pointing down; he stands inside it, looking for the moon. The salok ends on a question, not a slogan, and other lines of the Var answer it with the Guru, the lamp it opened with. An age can cut. Power can butcher. Truth can hide like the moon on a dark night. And still someone keeps searching the sky for it. That's today's line: a knife of an age.
screen: `KAL: THE DARK AGE BECOMES A BLADE.` · `THE KINGS HAVE BECOME BUTCHERS.` · `TRUTH'S MOON CAN'T BE SEEN.` · `NANAK SEARCHES IN THE DARK.` · then, large: `A KNIFE OF AN AGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind, one at a time, the people who hold power over your life, in your town, your country, your work, and instead of arguing with them in your head, picture the moon of truth rising over each, a small light in a dark sky. If you pray, ask God in your own way for honesty in those who lead; if you don't, simply wish it for them, and for the people under them.
The dark age is a knife. Guru Nanak's salok in Majh ki Var: the age cuts, kings are butchers, righteousness has flown, and truth's moon hides, while he keeps searching. Today's word.
screen: `THE DARK AGE IS A KNIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a knife of an age. Nanak's question still stands, and so does his searching. Same time tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1170 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM.`

1171.title: Hard to be called a Muslim
1171.word: Hard to be called a Muslim
1171.hook: it is hard to be called a true Muslim; first love the faith and let go of pride (Majh ki Var, ang 141)
1171.howItsDone: These saloks are sung and read as part of Majh ki Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in katha they are explained as Guru Nanak asking people of every faith to live what their own faith teaches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a knife of an age: kings turned butcher, truth's moon hidden, and Nanak still searching the dark. Today the ballad turns from kings to the name a person carries.

A cast-iron pan comes out of the back of a cupboard, orange with rust. Steel wool, hot water, patience, and slowly the dark metal shows again. Nobody calls it clean until it is. Guru Nanak lived among Hindus and Muslims, and in his ballad in Majh he speaks to his Muslim neighbors in the words of their own faith. He doesn't tell anyone to stop being a Muslim. He says something harder, in plain English: it's difficult to be called a Muslim. Only if you truly are one should you be called one.
screen: `A RUSTY PAN, SCOURED.` → `NANAK SPEAKS TO HIS NEIGHBORS.` → `HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: The salok goes on, not word for word. First, let the faith be sweet to you. Scrape away pride in your wealth, the way rust is scraped from metal. Become a true follower of the faith, and be rid of doubt about death and life. Accept God's will as above your head. Trust the Creator, and lose your self-importance. Be kind to every living being, says Nanak, and then you may be called a Muslim. Notice how high the bar is, and whose bar it is. Its words, din, faith; raza, God's will; mihar, mercy, are words his Muslim neighbors used for their own faith. He isn't laying a new standard over them; he's taking their own words seriously and asking that they be lived all the way through. A few lines before, on ang one hundred forty, he does the same with the outward signs. In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and honest living your Quran. Modesty, good conduct, truth: each a practice of the faith, lived inside. And the salok mocks no one. Elsewhere on this path Nanak asks the same of pandits and yogis: live what your name promises. Muslims here are honored by being held to their own best words. Notice the order, too. First, sweetness, before rules or outward signs. The salok calls this hard. It doesn't call it impossible. That's today's line: hard to be true.
screen: `FIRST, LET THE FAITH BE SWEET.` · `SCRAPE AWAY PRIDE LIKE RUST.` · `MERCY BE YOUR MOSQUE.` · `BE KIND TO EVERY BEING.` · then, large: `HARD TO BE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Name quietly what you're called: the faith you belong to, the one you're learning, or a simpler name like friend, parent, neighbor. Ask gently what that name promises, find one word in it, kindness, honesty, patience, mercy, and hold it for a few breaths. If you pray, offer that word to God in the way your own tradition prays.
Hard to be called a Muslim. Guru Nanak's salok in Majh ki Var: let the faith be sweet, scrape away pride, accept God's will, be kind to every being, and then be called by the name. Today's word.
screen: `HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hard to be true. Hard, and still worth the scouring, like that old pan. Until tomorrow.

1172.title: Majh ki Var close
1172.hook: a ballad that asks everyone to live up to their own name
1172.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Majh ki Var in kirtan and katha at the gurdwara, and teachers may linger on its saloks that hold believers of every name to the same plain honesty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hard to be true: it's hard to be called a Muslim, the salok said; first let the faith be sweet, then let pride go.

To take what belongs by right to someone else is pork to the Muslim and beef to the Hindu. That's a salok in Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, in plain English, not word for word. It names a food each of his neighbors refuses, and it doesn't ask either one to give that refusal up. It borrows the full weight of it and points it somewhere new: at the coin, the hour, the credit that was never yours. Two names, one measure.
screen: `ANOTHER'S RIGHT.` → `PORK TO ONE, BEEF TO THE OTHER.` → `TWO NAMES, ONE MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Look back over the Var as this path has walked it. It opened with the Guru as giver, a cool house of ice, a lamp. It named an age like a knife, where kings turn butcher. Yesterday it said it is hard to be called a Muslim, and asked that mercy be the mosque. Today's salok, on the same page as yesterday's, speaks to Muslim and Hindu in one breath, each in the terms of their own practice. It goes on, in paraphrase: the Guru and the pir will stand up for you only if you don't eat what is carrion. Talk alone carries no one to paradise; release comes from practicing truth. Adding spice to forbidden food doesn't make it lawful. Three things to notice. First, one measure for both. Neither neighbor is ranked above the other; each is held to a line they already keep, in a new place. Second, the new place is ordinary: not a shrine or a feast day, but what you take, a share, a seat, a turn in line, the credit for someone else's work. Third, words don't settle it. The ballad has done this from its first stanzas: holding a name, king, believer, Muslim, Hindu, up beside a life and asking whether the two match. Some readers hear it asking the same of anyone who carries a name, Sikhs included. A name is honored when the life under it takes nothing that isn't its own. That's today's line: live up to your name.
screen: `GIVER, KNIFE, HARD TO BE TRUE.` · `ONE MEASURE FOR TWO NEIGHBORS.` · `NOT A SHRINE: WHAT YOU TAKE.` · `TALK DOESN'T CARRY YOU.` · then, large: `LIVE UP TO YOUR NAME.`

segments.voice: Walk through the day ahead in your mind, the work, the meals, the talk, and look for one place where something not quite yours could slip into your hands: someone's turn, the credit for a shared idea, the last of something meant to be split. Don't judge it; just see yourself, at that moment, leaving it where it belongs. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath out.
Majh ki Var close. Guru Nanak's ballad in Raga Majh, a run of stanzas and saloks that holds each name, Muslim and Hindu alike, up against a life. Today's word.
Your line: live up to your name. The Var in Majh closes on that one measure. See you tomorrow.

1173.title: Kirat karo, deeper
1173.hook: honest work as spiritual practice, not only income
1173.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karo as earning a living honestly by their own effort, and Sikh teachers describe daily work, done truthfully, as part of a Sikh life rather than apart from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Var in Majh closed: another's right is pork to one neighbor, beef to the other. Your line was live up to your name.

Sawdust on the forearms. A plane sliding along a board, curls of wood dropping to the floor. Somewhere in Punjab, the story goes, a carpenter named Lalo worked like this all day, while a rich official named Malik Bhago threw a great feast down the road. Guru Nanak was invited to the feast. He ate the carpenter's plain bread instead. When the official demanded to know why, the story says, Nanak took bread from each table and squeezed. From Lalo's came milk. From the feast came blood. It's a story Sikhs tell, not a line from the Granth. But it asks today's question: what is the work of your hands made of?
screen: `A CARPENTER'S BREAD.` → `A RICH MAN'S FEAST.` → `MILK, AND BLOOD.`

segments.voice: One Sikh summary of Guru Nanak's way has three short phrases: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn by honest work; vand chhako, share what you have. This path met them before; this week each gets a deeper day, starting with work. Kirat means labor, the work of your own effort. Karo means do it. Under it sits a salok of Guru Nanak, in paraphrase: someone who calls himself a guru or a holy man and goes about begging, don't bow at his feet. The one who eats what he has earned by his own effort, and gives some of it from his hand, Nanak says, that one recognizes the path. Holiness isn't proven by leaving work behind. In this line, the one who has found the way has a paycheck, a harvest or a till, and something in their hand to give. Earning and the path aren't two rooms. They're the same room. That's why the Lalo story lands. It isn't against wealth; it's about where the bread came from. Bread made by honest hands carries something good. Bread made by squeezing other people carries what was squeezed. So kirat is more than having a job. It's how the job is done: the honest invoice, the full hour for the full wage, the repair done right when nobody would notice. Done that way, the work becomes part of the practice, not a break from it. That's today's line: work as prayer.
screen: `THREE PHRASES, ONE WAY.` · `KIRAT: THE WORK OF YOUR OWN EFFORT.` · `EARN, AND GIVE FROM THE HAND.` · `HOW THE JOB IS DONE.` · then, large: `WORK AS PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Choose one hour ahead, your job, cooking, cleaning, study, caring for someone, and set one intention for it: honest, whole, done well, nobody watching required. Rest your hands open on your knees, the hands that will do the work, and breathe slowly. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
Kirat karo. Earn by honest work, the labor of your own effort, done in a way that is itself part of the spiritual life. Today's word.
Your line: work as prayer. Lalo's plain bread was the meal Nanak chose. I'll be here tomorrow.

1174.title: Naam japo, deeper
1174.hook: remembrance as the root of everything else
1174.howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam japo through nitnem, the daily prayers, through simran, repeating Waheguru, and through kirtan; some rise in amrit vela, the hours before dawn, to begin the day with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat karo: earn by honest work, and give from the hand. Your line was work as prayer.

The morning after a storm, two old trees on one street. One is down across a lawn, its underside lifted into the air, a flat plate of soil and short roots. The one next to it, just as tall, still stands, missing a few branches. From above the ground they looked the same. The difference was underneath, where nobody could see it. Yesterday was the branches: honest work, out in the world. Tomorrow, the fruit: sharing. Today is the part underground.
screen: `TWO TREES, ONE STORM.` → `THE DIFFERENCE IS UNDERNEATH.` → `TODAY: THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Naam japo. Naam is the Name, the word Sikhs use for the presence of the One, not a label but something lived with. Japo means repeat it, remember it, keep it going. Guru Nanak's own lines show why it sits underneath. In the Japji, the morning prayer, he says, in paraphrase: in the ambrosial hours before dawn, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. That's amrit vela, the early hours some Sikhs keep for this. Remembrance comes first, before the work. In a hymn in Raga Asa that Sikhs sing in the evening prayer, there's a line short enough to carry: saying it, I live; forgetting it, I die. The Name isn't an extra. It's breath. And one more picture from the Japji: when hands and feet and body are covered in dirt, water washes them clean; when the mind is stained, it's washed by love of the Name. So remembering comes before the day, forgetting is a kind of dying, and the mind gets clean the way hands do, by going back to the water again and again. That's why it's the root. Honest work without it can turn hard. Sharing without it can turn proud. With it underneath, both have something to stand on when the wind comes. You don't see a root. You only see what it holds up. That's today's line: the root.

segments.voice: Think of the next piece of work waiting for you, a task, a call, a sink full of dishes, and before you touch it, go underneath it. On each breath, rest your attention on the One, however you understand that: if you pray, say Waheguru silently, once in and once out; if you don't, simply notice the breath as something given.
Naam japo. Remember the Name and keep remembering it, the part of Guru Nanak's way that sits underneath work and sharing. Today's word.

1175.title: Vand chhako, deeper
1175.hook: sharing as the shape of a life, not a donation
1175.howItsDone: Sikhs practice vand chhako through langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara where anyone may eat, through seva, and through dasvandh, setting aside a portion of what they earn to share.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam japo: remembrance underneath everything, like roots under a tree. Today, the fruit.

A boy is handed a bag of coins and sent to market. His father's instruction is simple: make a good deal, a true bargain, something that will turn a profit. On the road, the story says, the boy meets holy men who have gone without food. He looks at the coins, and at them, buys food and feeds them, and walks home with an empty bag. His father is furious. The boy is Nanak, and the story gives his answer: that was the true bargain, sacha sauda, the true deal. Today, the third of the three phrases.

segments.voice: Vand chhako. Vand means divide, share out. Chhako means eat, take your portion. The order is the teaching: share, and eat. Not eat, and then give away whatever's left over. The sharing is built into the meal itself. That's the difference between a donation and a shape. A donation is something you do once in a while, on top of a life. A shape is the life. Guru Nanak's salok from two days ago already holds it: the one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives something from his hand, recognizes the path. Earning and giving, in one breath. And Sikh life made that shape visible. Tradition says Guru Nanak's community at Kartarpur farmed together and ate together, and it traces langar, the free kitchen, to that: a meal served to anyone who walks in, everyone on the same floor, eating the same food. Nobody fills out a form to prove they're hungry. Nobody is asked their faith. That's vand chhako at the scale of a community. The Sacha Sauda story makes the same point in one afternoon. The father wanted a deal that turned a profit. The boy saw a deal that fed people, and called that the true one. So the deeper version of sharing isn't how much you give. It's whether giving comes first, before the asking, before the leftovers, before anyone has to explain themselves. That's today's line: share first.

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who could use something you have, not necessarily money: time, a meal, a ride, a skill, a phone call, attention. Notice whether they would ever ask, since some people never do, and picture yourself offering it before they have to. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.
Vand chhako. Share, and eat: the sharing built into the meal and into the shape of a life, not added afterward. Today's word.
Your line: share first. The true bargain is the one that feeds someone. See you tomorrow.

1176.title: Nanak's teachings close
1176.hook: a dialogue, an alphabet, a lament, the months, and three pillars
1176.howItsDone: Sikhs meet Guru Nanak's longer compositions, such as the Sidh Gosht, Oankar, Patti and Barah Maha, in kirtan and in katha at the gurdwara, sometimes studied over a run of sessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vand chhako: share, and eat, the sharing built into the meal. Today the whole stretch of Guru Nanak's longer teachings comes to a close.

Suppose you could keep one sentence from the last several weeks, and only one. A circle of yogis on a mountain asking a stranger who he is. A pandit's alphabet turned into a poem. A child's writing tablet, one letter at a time. A lament for a city attacked and the women who suffered there. A year of months, each one aching. A ballad that holds every name up against a life. Three short phrases about remembering, working and sharing. That's a lot of road. Today, a look back down it.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE TO KEEP.` → `A MOUNTAIN, AN ALPHABET, A LAMENT.` → `MONTHS, A BALLAD, THREE PHRASES.`

segments.voice: Lay the pieces side by side and one move keeps repeating: Guru Nanak takes something outward and turns it inward, without throwing it away. In the Sidh Gosht, the yogis wear earrings and a patched coat; he makes the Word the earring, worn within, and turns the coat into seeing the One in everything. In the Oankar, a learned man reads and argues; Nanak asks whether he has understood, and calls true learning reflection on the Name. In the Patti, a school slate becomes a lesson for the soul, one letter at a time. In the Babarvani, faith doesn't look away; it names the pain of ordinary people caught in an invasion. In his twelve months in Raga Tukhari, every season becomes a way of longing for the Beloved. In the Var in Majh, a name becomes a promise to live up to. And in the three phrases, a job, a meal and a breath each become practice. So that is Nanak's way, as these weeks have shown it. Not leaving the world. Living in it like a lotus in water, untouched, and making every ordinary thing point somewhere. One more detail before new ground. Guru Nanak's hymns are signed with his name, Nanak. The Gurus whose hymns follow his in the Granth signed them Nanak too, and a heading tells you whose voice it is: Mahala one, Mahala two, and on. The name carries on into the next voice. That's today's line: Nanak's way.
screen: `OUTWARD TURNED INWARD.` · `EARRINGS, SLATES, MONTHS AND NAMES.` · `LIVING IN THE WORLD, UNTOUCHED.` · `THE NAME CARRIES ON.` · then, large: `NANAK'S WAY.`

segments.voice: Let the stretch pass by again, the mountain conversation, the alphabet, the tablet, the lament, the months, the ballad, the three phrases, and don't choose the one that sounds wisest. Notice which one keeps coming back to you, and hold it on the breath for a while. If you pray, say Waheguru quietly on each breath out.
Nanak's teachings close. A dialogue, an alphabet, a lament, the months, a ballad and three pillars, all turning the outward world inward. Today's word.
Your line: nanak's way. Next comes the voice that carried his name on. Until tomorrow.
